newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Fletcher says 2nd half matched 1st half.
newsitem.headline: Fletcher says 2nd half matched 1st half.

text.p: New Zealand conglomerate Fletcher Challenge Ltd said on Thursday the group had experienced a similar second half for 1996/97 to its first half with mixed performances from its four divisions.
"It (1996/97) was a distinct improvement for Energy, it was around similar for Building and Forests and and it was decidedly worse for Paper," chief executive Hugh Fletcher told reporters.
"It was a year of pretty similar halves in contrast to the previous year," he said after addressing a Securities Institute of Australia briefing.
Fletcher was upbeat on prospects for the next financial year, saying he believed Pulp and Paper was on a recovery.
"We believe we have sorted out a number of our issues in Building, we are going through a large merger in Forests ... and we think we will have another good year in Energy."

Fletcher Challenge, which reports the results for each of the four listed divisions separately as well consolidated group results, boosted consolidated net profit to NZ$192 million in the first half ended December 31 from NZ$130 million a year earlier.
Fletcher said the group's best performer in 1996/97 was the Energy division, adding that it planned to produce 50 million barrels of oil equivalent (boe) in 1997/98.

He said Fletcher Challenge Energy Ltd had developed strong businesses in New Zealand and Canada and wanted production, which had grown 40 percent a year, to continue at a similar rate with a third arena currently being developed in Brunei.

Beyond that, it would be interested in entering the Western Australian energy market if it could do so at a reasonable price and while the company had made no bids yet it was actively looking at some co-generation possibilities there, he said.
Fletcher said that if the announced paper prices for the third 1997 calendar quarter were to apply, then Fletcher Challenge Paper Ltd should return to profit in 1997/98.
The industry had to ascertain whether or not improving prices were going to be sustainable or whether they were in an inventory cycle, he said.
